chief_complaint: severe squeezing chest pain waking me up from sleep at 4 AM every morning
hpi_details: 4-week history of highly predictable, severe retrosternal squeezing chest pain that occurs reliably between 3 AM and 5 AM while sleeping in bed, waking her up in severe distress. Episodes last 10 to 15 minutes, radiate to her left shoulder, and resolve spontaneously. Curiously, she can run 5 kilometres on the treadmill at the gym during the afternoon without experiencing any chest pain or shortness of breath whatsoever. Has a heavy cigarette smoking history.
ideas: thinks smoking cigarettes late at night makes her heart arteries spasm while sleeping
concerns: terrified she will have a massive fatal heart attack in her sleep when alone
expectations: wants calcium channel blockers and a clear explanation for why her heart hurts only when sleeping
pmh: migraine headaches, Raynaud's phenomenon of fingers in cold weather, no diabetes or hypertension
medications: sumatriptan PRN for migraines (reports taking one last week which triggered a severe nocturnal angina attack)
social_hx: smokes 20 cigarettes/day since age 18, drinks 6 units/week, graphic designer

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Prinzmetal (Vasospastic) Angina is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes avoiding vasoconstrictive triggers such as sumatriptan and generally avoiding beta-blockers, especially non-selective agents, which can worsen coronary spasm, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: severe squeezing chest pain waking me up from sleep at 4 AM every morning

Key HPI features: 4-week history of highly predictable, severe retrosternal squeezing chest pain that occurs reliably between 3 AM and 5 AM while sleeping in bed, waking her up in severe distress. Episodes last 10 to 15 minutes, radiate to her left shoulder, and resolve spontaneously. Curiously, she can run 5 kilometres on the treadmill at the gym during the afternoon without experiencing any chest pain or shortness of breath whatsoever. Has a heavy cigarette smoking history.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals and physical exam: completely normal. 12-lead resting ECG: normal sinus rhythm. Outpatient or emergency room ECG captured during an early-morning attack: shows transient, reversible ST-segment elevation that completely resolves when the pain subsides (or after sublingual GTN). CT Coronary Angiography or invasive coronary angiography: reveals completely smooth, patent epicardial coronary arteries without obstructive atherosclerotic plaques, but hyper-reactivity to provocation testing (e.g., acetylcholine or ergonovine infusion inducing focal coronary artery spasm).
Relevant background/PMH: migraine headaches, Raynaud's phenomenon of fingers in cold weather, no diabetes or hypertension
Current medications: sumatriptan PRN for migraines (reports taking one last week which triggered a severe nocturnal angina attack)
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Prinzmetal (Vasospastic) Angina.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Acute coronary syndrome without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Spasm can cause dangerous arrhythmias — syncope with the pain is a red flag.
management_principles: Avoid vasoconstrictive triggers such as sumatriptan and generally avoid beta-blockers, especially non-selective agents, which can worsen coronary spasm

Initiate high-dose Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., diltiazem 240mg OD or amlodipine 10mg OD) as first-line therapy to relax vascular smooth muscle, combined with long-acting nitrates (e.g., isosorbide mononitrate) and PRN sublingual GTN spray for acute attacks
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

source_refs.title: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease

reference_soap.subjective: 36F heavy smoker with Raynaud's/migraine presents with recurrent nocturnal rest angina waking her at 4 AM, with completely normal daytime exercise tolerance. Exacerbated by triptan ingestion.
reference_soap.objective: Vitals and physical exam: completely normal. 12-lead resting ECG: normal sinus rhythm. Outpatient or emergency room ECG captured during an early-morning attack: shows transient, reversible ST-segment elevation that completely resolves when the pain subsides (or after sublingual GTN). CT Coronary Angiography or invasive coronary angiography: reveals completely smooth, patent epicardial coronary arteries without obstructive atherosclerotic plaques, but hyper-reactivity to provocation testing (e.g., acetylcholine or ergonovine infusion inducing focal coronary artery spasm).
reference_soap.assessment: Prinzmetal's Variant Angina (Vasospastic Angina) due to focal coronary artery vasospasm. DDx: unstable angina / atherosclerotic ACS, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (nocturnal reflux), panic attacks, obstructive sleep apnoea induced angina.
reference_soap.plan: Avoid vasoconstrictive triggers such as sumatriptan and generally avoid beta-blockers, especially non-selective agents, which can worsen coronary spasm. Initiate high-dose Calcium Channel Blockers (e.g., diltiazem 240mg OD or amlodipine 10mg OD) as first-line therapy to relax vascular smooth muscle, combined with long-acting nitrates (e.g., isosorbide mononitrate) and PRN sublingual GTN spray for acute attacks. Mandatory urgent smoking cessation support (tobacco is the primary trigger for endothelial dysfunction and vasospasm).

learning_objectives: Identify the classical circadian presentation of Prinzmetal's variant angina: rest angina waking patients in the early morning with preserved daytime exercise tolerance
Explain the physiological mechanism of coronary vasospasm linked to generalized vasospastic disorders (Raynaud's, migraines)
Recognise medications that can precipitate or worsen vasospasm, including triptans and especially non-selective beta-blockers
Formulate first-line vasodilator prophylaxis utilizing calcium channel blockers and nitrates coupled with mandatory smoking cessation

teaching.one_liner: Coronary spasm rather than fixed narrowing — pain at rest, typically in the early hours, in someone who exercises without symptoms.
red_flags: Spasm can cause dangerous arrhythmias — syncope with the pain is a red flag

must_ask.say: Does it wake you at a particular time — the early hours of the morning?

must_ask.objective: Pain at rest but not on exertion
must_ask.say: Can you exercise without any chest pain at all?
Do you smoke, and how much?
Do you use any recreational drugs, particularly cocaine?
Have you been given a spray or tablet under the tongue, and did it help?
How would you describe it — sharp, crushing, burning, tight?
